v.why: When edge 5 is absent, the direct edge 0->3 carries more of the signal to the output, so upgrading it to a 3x3 conv helps more.
With no direct input-to-output edge, activating edge 5 can restore a path to the output and give a large gain (experiments 55, 81).
Deleting edge 3 costs more when it held a strong 3x3 conv than when it held a weak op such as pooling.
Replacing a 3x3 conv on the final edge with parameter-free pooling removes key capacity (experiments 18, 22).
When node 1 is dead, edge 1 is the only way to compute at node 2, so a conv there matters more (experiment 26).
Replacing a pooling op with a conv adds learnable capacity, which gains more than replacing an existing conv (experiment 30).
Swapping a direct 3x3 conv for an identity loses capacity, whereas replacing pooling or none with skip is often neutral or positive (experiments 47, 61 vs 54, 85).
If edge 1 is already missing, removing edge 0 also cuts nodes 1 and 2 off from the input and collapses the cell's depth.
Adding a conv where there was no edge both adds capacity and connects node 2 to the output (experiments 2, 70).
When edge 0 is none, node 1 carries zero signal, so any op placed on edge 4 has little effect.

raw:
Most of these follow from how the cell is wired. Node 3 is fed by edges 3, 4 and 5, and an edit that cuts or restores a path to it swings accuracy by tens of points (experiments 19, 30, 44, 55, 81, 82). Convolutions are the useful operations. Replacing one with avg_pool or skip_connect usually hurts (experiments 18, 22, 47, 61, 80). And when edge 0 is 'none', node 1 carries nothing, so edges 2 and 4 have nothing to pass on.

These are predictions from that reasoning, not tested results. Hypotheses 1–7 and 9 are partly supported by the experiments cited in each line. Hypotheses 8 and 10 rest on the wiring argument alone, since the 100 experiments include no edge 0 → none edit with edge 1 = 'none' and no edge 4 → nor_conv_3x3 edit with edge 0 = 'none'. Neither has been checked against the benchmark yet.
